Did Corporate Due Diligence Work in the DRC?

Evaluating the OECD Due Diligence Guidance (2016) through the lens of the M&E Framework (2022)

This overview presents the core empirical findings in five sections: (A) DD's scope and leverage constraints, (B) how the two-sided mechanism works, (C) why aggregate violence trends cannot test DD's effectiveness, (D) econometric evidence of DD's treatment effect in areas where it operated, and (E) the underlying mechanism through which the 4 measures work.

A
DD Scope and Leverage: Where Corporate Influence Works
Annex II covers all armed actors, but companies have differential leverage to change behavior

This analysis operationalises the OECD Monitoring & Evaluation Framework (2022) — the official theory of change for the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas (3rd ed., 2016). The framework posits a supply-chain mechanism: downstream purchasing pressure → smelter compliance → mine-level interventions (iTSCi's 4-pillar programme) → reduced armed group mineral access → less violence. While Annex II of the DDG covers risks from all armed actors—including state security forces and foreign-sponsored groups—companies' ability to shape markets and influence ultimate outcomes is modulated depending on armed actor type:

✓ DD has direct leverage over
Non-state armed groups dependent on mineral revenues for operations and territorial control. Supply chain exit threats can cut off their financing, forcing behavioral change.
⚠ DD has indirect influence over
State security forces (FARDC), foreign-sponsored groups (M23), and other actors where purchasing decisions do not directly change behavior. DD flags these risks but requires complementary interventions: diplomatic pressure, peacekeeping, host government engagement, and legal accountability mechanisms.

Critics argue DD may have merely displaced violence (the "balloon effect"—reducing violence in one location causes it to emerge elsewhere) (Parker & Vadheim, 2017; Stoop et al., 2018). If DD's direct leverage worked as intended, one would expect reduced violence in areas where iTSCi operated compared to similar areas without iTSCi. Step D tests this prediction using a difference-in-differences design.

Evaluations that judge DD against aggregate violence trends will fail to isolate DD's effect from confounding regional conflicts. DD identifies and reports all Annex II risks, but supply chain pressure operates locally — its effectiveness must be tested using localized comparisons, not aggregate time series where multiple conflicts co-evolve.

B
How Due Diligence Works: A Two-Sided Mechanism
DD requires both upstream traceability (iTSCi) and downstream demand (purchasing commitments)

DD operates through a two-sided supply-chain mechanism:

📦 Supply Side (Upstream)
iTSCi operates mine-level interventions: Traceability (bagging/tagging), incident reporting, multi-stakeholder risk mitigation, and community policing. Scaled from 437 mines (2014) to 1,395 mines (2022). (See Step E for detailed mechanism.)
🏭 Demand Side (Downstream)
Companies preferentially purchase from audited smelters: Certified smelters gained 82 more downstream customers (36% premium) than non-certified smelters (2014-2025), creating market incentives.

The mechanism: Downstream companies preferentially purchase from audited smelters → RMI audits smelters → Smelters demand iTSCi-tagged minerals → iTSCi enrolls mines and implements 4-pillar programme → Mine operators comply to maintain market access → Reduced armed group interference → Less violence. Both sides are necessary — upstream interventions without downstream demand create compliance incentives that lack market value; downstream commitments without upstream infrastructure have nothing to verify. Buying companies influence mine-level behavior indirectly through procurement practices that reward compliance.

→ See RMI smelter conformance trends in Supply Chain tab

All three actor categories increased together. Pairwise correlations: Local ↔ FARDC (r=0.74), Local ↔ Foreign (r=0.80), FARDC ↔ Foreign (r=0.89). Local armed group violence grew fastest in absolute terms (+340%, driven by a sharp 2022 spike), FARDC grew moderately (+46%), and Foreign actors grew steadily (+72%). E
Mechanism: How iTSCi's 4 Measures Prevent and Mitigate Conflict
The underlying causal mechanism for conflict reduction at enrolled mines
iTSCi programme documentation; OECD M&E Framework (2022)

Mechanism: The underlying mechanism for conflict prevention and mitigation lies in iTSCi's 4-measure programme that enrolled mines implement. These measures create transparency, enable incident response, and facilitate collective action to reduce armed group interference.

1. Continuous Monitoring & Traceability
Ongoing monitoring of mine sites; bagging and tagging of 3T minerals from mine to smelter. Creates transparency along the mineral supply chain and serves as the starting point for reporting risks.
2. Incident Reporting Mechanism
System for recording and following up on incidents, including whistleblowing hotline promoted in mining communities. Captures and documents armed group presence, child labor, and other Annex II risks.
3. Multi-Stakeholder Committees
Facilitation of local and provincial committees bringing together miners, village chiefs, territorial administrators, army/police chiefs, and civil society. Provides platform for participatory risk resolution and mitigation.
4. Joint Risk Mitigation Measures
Development of joint strategies involving mining operators, government, security forces, and civil society (deterrence, sanctions, community policing). Promotes buy-in and strengthens local enforcement capacity.

How downstream demand creates the incentive: Mine operators comply with these 4 measures to maintain access to certified supply chains. Downstream companies preferentially purchase from audited smelters, who in turn demand iTSCi-tagged minerals, creating market pressure for mine-level compliance.

⚠️ Contextual Factor: Actor Substitution at Mines (2010–2022)

During the same period iTSCi scaled up (2010–2022), IPIS mine visits documented a shift in actor presence: non-state militia interference declined from 36% to 12% (↓65% relative decline), while FARDC presence increased from 30% to 39% (↑32% relative increase).

Important: This actor substitution occurred concurrently with iTSCi's rollout but represents a separate governance dynamic—state security forces filling vacuums left by declining non-state groups. Whether this was caused by the 4 measures, FARDC counter-insurgency operations, or both cannot be determined from mine visit data alone (n=725 visits, non-random sample). The econometric evidence in Step D provides the causal validation of DD's effectiveness. FARDC presence at mines is a governance problem (state rent-extraction), not an insurgent financing problem, and falls outside the supply-chain leverage mechanism.

Synthesis

DD achieved a 61% reduction in violence in treated mining areas (econometric evidence, Step D). Aggregate violence trends cannot demonstrate effectiveness — all actor categories co-evolved during iTSCi's rollout, making it impossible to separate DD's effect from confounding regional conflicts.

The data are consistent with the theory of change that corporate due diligence reduced violence where it operated, as shown by the difference-in-differences analysis. However, aggregate patterns show all violence increasing together (correlations r=0.74-0.89), reflecting broader regional instability beyond any single intervention's control. Claims of DD's "failure" based on aggregate trends ignore this complexity and the econometric evidence of localized effectiveness.

📚 Case Studies: For detailed examples of how demilitarization works in practice, see the Case Studies tab, which examines Bisie (military + LSM interventions) and Nyabibwe (iTSCi pilot site demonstrating traceability + market mechanisms).

Forward-looking implications: The evidence suggests DD can be expanded to remaining high-conflict provinces (Nord-Kivu, Ituri) where it should reduce local armed group violence. However, LSM grew from 0% (2016) to 70% (2022) of 3T production, shifting output away from artisanal supply chains. As production industrializes, the share accessible to mine-level traceability shrinks—requiring adaptation of DD frameworks to industrial mining contexts.

Complementary interventions needed: Peacekeeping operations to counter M23/ADF, diplomatic pressure on Rwanda, FARDC professionalization to reduce state-led mine interference, and adaptation of due diligence systems to industrial mining operations.

📍 The Key Question

Can we attribute aggregate violence trends to DD's success or failure? No—because multiple conflict types evolved simultaneously. Local armed groups (+340%) rose alongside FARDC violence (+46%) and foreign militia activity (+72%). High correlations (r=0.74–0.89) between categories indicate shared regional drivers (M23 resurgence, FARDC counter-insurgency operations, regional spillover). Testing DD requires disaggregating actor types and comparing treated vs. untreated mining areas.

This section: (1) Shows what violence types are measured, (2) Disaggregates trends by actor category, (3) Classifies resource-linked vs. other conflict, (4) Documents armed group presence at mine sites. The econometric evidence testing DD's causal effect is in the Overview tab.

2. Aggregate Trends by Actor Type

Violence disaggregated by armed actor category. Shows why aggregate trends cannot isolate DD's effect—all categories increased together with high correlations.

Resource-Linked Violence Trends by Actor Category
Conflict events disaggregated by armed actor type, 2010–2022
ACLED, Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, 2010–2022; author typology

All three actor categories increased together. Pairwise correlations: Local ↔ FARDC (r=0.74), Local ↔ Foreign (r=0.80), FARDC ↔ Foreign (r=0.89). Local armed group violence grew fastest in absolute terms (+340%, driven by a sharp 2022 spike), FARDC grew moderately (+46%), and Foreign actors grew steadily (+72%). These high correlations indicate common regional drivers (M23 resurgence, FARDC counter-insurgency, regional instability), making it impossible to isolate DD's effect from aggregate patterns alone.

The 2022 spike explained: Research indicates the surge in local armed group violence (+109%, 432→902 events) was driven primarily by escalating CODECO attacks in Ituri province. CODECO—an ethnic Lendu militia coalition—intensified attacks on IDP camps and civilians throughout 2022, killing an estimated 400+ civilians by mid-year according to UN OCHA. This violence coincided with FARDC military operations that displaced militants, who then exploited security vacuums to attack civilian areas. The spike represents genuine local armed group activity escalation, not M23 spillover or coding changes. Aggregate trends cannot test DD's effectiveness because multiple regional conflicts (CODECO ethnic violence, M23 resurgence, ADF expansion) evolved simultaneously.

⚠️ Data limitation — Gold vs. 3T: The "Local armed groups" category includes substantial gold-related violence not covered in this research. This analysis focuses on 3T minerals (tin, tantalum, tungsten); gold mining operates under similar DD frameworks but is not examined here. CODECO (810 events, 16% of local violence) fights primarily over gold mines in Ituri with zero presence at 3T mine sites (IPIS data). Research by Stoop et al. (2018) and Parker & Vadheim (2017) suggests displacement of armed groups from 3T to gold sectors, indicating that an estimated 16-56% of local armed group violence may be gold-related. ACLED's "resource-linked" methodology includes all minerals, meaning the data captures both 3T and gold conflicts, though this research focuses only on 3T interventions.

3. Detailed Conflict Type Classification

Five-category typology showing total events, fatalities, and lethality. Click any category card to see full definition and actor list.

Local armed groups dominate resource-linked violence (5,061 events, 42% of total), followed by DRC State Forces (2,908 events, 24%) and Transnational groups (2,241 events, 19%). Rwandan Proxy conflicts account for 1,613 events (14%). By province, Sud-Kivu and Nord-Kivu account for the majority of violence across all categories, while Maniema—with deepest iTSCi coverage—shows minimal violence despite high mine density.

Resource-linked violence represents 36% of all conflict events in the dataset (11,882 of 32,842 total events). Lethality by type
Average fatalities per event — which category kills most per incident
ACLED, Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, 2010–2022; author typology

Transnational armed groups are the most lethal (3.39 fatalities/event), followed by DRC State Forces (2.64/event) and MONUSCO peacekeeping interventions (2.37/event). 5. Armed Groups at Mine Sites

Direct observation from IPIS field visits. Shows which armed actors are physically present at mine sites vs. those who engage in regional violence but avoid mines.

Armed Group Typology at Mine Sites
Classification of armed actors at mine sites — IPIS data, all visits
IPIS Research, DRC Mine Visit Database (all years)
DRC State Forces (504 visits, 67%) Local Armed Groups (195 visits, 26%) Foreign Armed Groups (25 visits, 3%)

State forces dominate mine sites: DRC State Forces (FARDC + Police) account for 67% of armed actor presence at mine visits—2.6× more than local armed groups. FARDC's "undisciplined elements" (241 visits) represents active interference, while "no interference" (105 visits) indicates presence without predation. Foreign armed groups show minimal mine-site presence (3%), consistent with their focus on terror/atrocity rather than mine-site predation.

Top Armed Groups by Mine Presence
Named groups recorded across all IPIS mine visits (up to 3 per mine)
IPIS Research, DRC Mine Visit Database (all years)

FARDC dominates by a wide margin (393 visits), followed by local militias like Raia Mutomboki (85 visits) and Mai-Mai groups. Foreign armed groups (M23, FDLR, ADF) appear infrequently at mine sites despite their prominence in regional violence. This gap between mine presence and conflict visibility indicates that foreign militias engage in territorial/political violence but do not systematically control mine sites.

Foreign Militia Sponsorship in Conflict Events
ACLED events classified by foreign sponsorship — 2010–2022
ACLED, Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project; author coding

Foreign-sponsored militias account for 21% of conflict events (3,737 events), primarily M23 and allied groups backed by Rwanda. The majority of violence (46%, 8,153 events) shows no evidence of foreign sponsorship—these are domestic conflicts driven by local grievances, land disputes, and resource competition. The "Not applicable" category (29%, 5,158 events) includes state violence and non-factional events. FARDC has been recoded as domestic; FDLR shows "no evidence" as Rwandan diaspora support does not constitute active state military sponsorship.

⚠ Structural transformation: From 2019 onward, industrial mining (LSM) entered 3T production at scale, growing from 28% (2019) to 70% (2022) of total output. This shift has implications for due diligence systems like iTSCi, which target artisanal supply chains. As production industrializes, the share accessible to mine-level traceability shrinks — industrial operators follow different regulatory frameworks (mining codes, industrial permits) than artisanal miners.

Market Advantage of Audited Smelters
Average downstream customers (SEC issuers) per smelter: Certified vs. Non-certified
Baik et al. (2024), Park et al. analysis of SEC Form SD filings, 2014-2025

Finding: Certified smelters gained an average of 82 more downstream customers than non-certified smelters (36% premium) over 2014-2025. This demonstrates that downstream companies preferentially source from audited smelters, creating market incentives for certification. Analysis controls for smelter and country×year fixed effects. Supply Chain Insights
Key findings from the data
UN Comtrade; RMI SoR list; iTSCi programme data

The "first mile" refers to the segment of the supply chain from artisanal mine site to first point of sale — the point at which minerals enter formal trade. It is where armed group interference, child labour, and environmental violations are most likely to occur, and where due diligence frameworks have the least visibility. Certification and qualification schemes (BGR, IPIS) attempt to audit this segment directly.

Among inspected mines, 86% are Green — but this only covers a fraction of all operating mines. The 'not inspected' gap is the critical blind spot in responsible sourcing.

Armed Presence by Mineral Type

IPIS Research, DRC Mine Visit Database (all years)

Gold mines show higher armed presence (56% vs 33% for 3T minerals), but most gold visits are in Sud-Kivu (65%) and Nord-Kivu (37%) — the two highest-conflict provinces. Within the same province the gap largely disappears (Nord-Kivu: gold 37% vs 3T 32%). The difference likely reflects where gold mines are located, not the mineral itself.

The Coverage–Violence Paradox
iTSCi mines enrolled by 2022 vs. resource-linked events 2018–2022 by province. Note: iTSCi figure is a 2022 snapshot; many mines enrolled after 2018 were not covered for the full event window.
iTSCi programme data; ACLED, 2018–2022; author coding

Maniema — deepest iTSCi penetration (509 mines) — had only 85 resource-linked events over five years. Nord-Kivu — last to join, thinnest coverage (218 mines) — had 3,916. Correlation is striking; the coverage gap maps almost exactly onto the violence gap.

Average treatment effect on treated (ATT) by province — econometric estimates
Christensen et al. (2025), difference-in-differences analysis using ACLED and iTSCi data, 2009–2022

Treatment effects concentrated in high-conflict provinces. Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Tanganyika, and Lualaba show statistically significant violence reductions where iTSCi operated. Maniema shows reduction but not statistically significant. Haut-Katanga shows moderate non-significant reductions. Haut-Lomami shows small positive coefficient (possible outlier). This pattern suggests DD's effectiveness is strongest where conflict risk was historically higher—iTSCi reduced violence most in precisely the provinces where violence was most severe.

When DD Impact Was Strongest: Temporal Dynamics
Estimated treatment effect over time showing largest reductions during high-conflict periods
Christensen et al. (2025), time-varying ATT estimates

Largest violence reductions occurred June 2019–June 2022, a period marked by significant increases in violence in untreated mining areas. This is intuitive: there is greater scope to reduce violence during periods of regional instability. DD's protective effect is most visible when baseline violence is high—iTSCi-enrolled areas were shielded from the violence surges that affected non-enrolled areas during this period.

No "Balloon Effect": Spillover Benefits, Not Displacement
Testing whether iTSCi displaced violence to neighboring untreated areas
Christensen et al. (2025), spillover analysis using treatment-adjacent control cells

Critics argue DD may merely displace violence (the "balloon effect"—reducing violence in one location causes it to emerge elsewhere). Econometric tests directly examined whether violence increased in untreated mining areas adjacent to iTSCi-enrolled sites.

Finding: Violence declined in treatment-adjacent areas, not increased. iTSCi's arrival reduced violent incidents in neighboring untreated cells. This suggests positive spillover—iTSCi's activities and coordination with local stakeholders created security improvements that extended beyond directly enrolled mine sites.

Robustness: Results remain negative (violence reduction) when excluding treatment-adjacent controls from the comparison group. If displacement occurred, removing these adjacent areas should weaken the estimated effect. Instead, the ATT becomes more negative, confirming no balloon effect.

Child Labor Trends at Mine Sites
Percentage of IPIS mine visits observing children under 15 present
IPIS Research, DRC Mine Visit Database (adapted from Gonzalez Torres et al. 2025, Figure 22)

⚠ Persistent issue: Child observation rates at mines show an increasing trend from 10.5% (2013) to 33.8% (2022), with a temporary decline in 2021. This data captures presence at point-in-time visits, not necessarily active labor. IPIS/ULULA (2019) and PRG et al. (2020) found no conclusive impact of DDPs on child labor rates—improvements were noted but couldn't be attributed to DDP presence. Note: No evaluations conducted in 2016-2017.

Occupational Safety: Accidents at DDP vs Non-DDP Sites
Comparison of mine safety conditions between DDP and non-DDP sites
IPIS/ULULA (2019); PRG et al. (2020)

Mixed results from different measurement approaches: IPIS/ULULA (2019) found fewer self-reported accidents at DDP sites (41% of sites reported accidents) vs non-DDP sites (47%), based on mine visit observations. However, PRG et al. (2020) found no significant differences in extraction conditions or documented injury counts between DDP and non-DDP sites when measured through household surveys. Fatal accidents were rare across all mines. The different findings likely reflect different measurement methodologies (observational site assessments vs. household injury reports) rather than contradictory evidence. Overall, this suggests OHS improvements require broader structural interventions beyond supply chain due diligence alone.

Econometric Methodology: Measuring Causal Impact
Difference-in-differences design to isolate iTSCi's treatment effect from confounding factors
Christensen et al. (2025), Appendix Section A2; Statistical methods based on Liu et al. (2022)

Evaluating due diligence (DD) effectiveness requires isolating its causal effect from confounding regional trends. Simply comparing violence before and after DD implementation conflates DD's impact with other simultaneous changes (e.g., military operations, peacekeeping, elections). This analysis employs a difference-in-differences (DiD) design using geographic cells as the unit of analysis, comparing changes in violence at iTSCi-enrolled mine sites versus comparable non-enrolled sites over time.

📊 Data Sources
iTSCi Programme Data (2012-2022): Mine-level enrollment records showing exact months each mine entered the programme. Provides treatment assignment and timing.

IPIS Mine Database (2009-2022): Geographic coordinates of 3T mine sites across eastern DRC, used to match mines to PRIO-GRID cells.

ACLED Conflict Events (2009-2023): Geolocated violent incidents including battles, explosions, violence against civilians. Dependent variable: monthly violent event counts per cell.
🗺️ Unit of Analysis: PRIO-GRID Cells
Geographic cells (0.5° × 0.5° latitude/longitude, ~55km × 55km at equator) serve as analysis units. Each cell may contain zero, one, or multiple mine sites.

Treatment assignment: A cell is "treated" in month t if ≥1 mine within it is enrolled in iTSCi by month t.

Sample: 304 cells containing 3T mines, observed monthly from Jan 2009 to Dec 2022 (168 months) = 51,072 cell-month observations.
🎯 Identification Strategy: The Counterfactual Problem

The fundamental challenge: We observe violence with iTSCi at treated cells, but we cannot directly observe what would have happened at those same cells without iTSCi (the counterfactual). A simple before-after comparison fails because violence trends may reflect regional factors unrelated to iTSCi.

DiD Solution: Assume that absent iTSCi, three factors affect violent incidents in cell i during month t:

Violencei,t = αi + βt + εi,t
αi: Time-invariant cell characteristics (geology, terrain, ethnic composition)
βt: Common shocks affecting all cells in month t (national elections, regional military operations)
εi,t: Idiosyncratic noise unrelated to iTSCi

DiD estimates αi and βt using only untreated observations (cells before iTSCi arrival + cells never enrolled), then constructs counterfactual violence for treated cells. The Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) = Actual violence in treated cells − Estimated counterfactual violence.

⚠ Critical Assumption: Parallel Trends
DiD requires that treated and control cells would have experienced similar violence trends absent treatment. We cannot test this directly (counterfactual is unobservable), but we can examine pre-treatment trends. If treated cells showed systematically different violence trajectories before iTSCi arrived, the parallel trends assumption fails.

Robustness check: Event study specifications show no statistically significant differential trends in the years before iTSCi enrollment, supporting the parallel trends assumption.
⚙️ Estimation Method: Liu et al. (2022) Estimator
We employ the Liu, Wang, & Xu (2022) matrix completion estimator for staggered adoption DiD:
  • Handles staggered treatment: iTSCi rolled out gradually (2012-2022), with different cells treated at different times
  • Allows time-varying effects: Treatment effects may evolve as iTSCi matures at a site
  • Robust to heterogeneity: Does not impose constant treatment effects across all cells
  • Uses only never-treated/not-yet-treated as controls: Avoids "forbidden comparisons" that bias standard two-way fixed effects models
Output: Estimated ATT for each treated cell-month, aggregated to produce overall ATT, provincial ATT, and temporal ATT estimates shown in charts above.
🎈 Testing for Displacement ("Balloon Effect")
Appendix Table 3: Excluding Adjacent Controls
If iTSCi displaces violence to neighboring cells, removing treatment-adjacent cells from the control group should weaken the estimated effect (removing the most violence-affected controls). Instead, ATT becomes more negative (stronger violence reduction), rejecting displacement.

Appendix Table 4: Indirect Effects on Adjacent Untreated Cells
Directly tests whether violence increased in never-treated cells adjacent to treated cells after iTSCi arrived. Finds negative spillover: violence declined in neighboring untreated cells, suggesting positive security externalities rather than displacement.
Interpreting the 61% reduction: This is the estimated causal effect of iTSCi enrollment on violent incidents in treated cells, averaging across all treated cell-months from 2012-2022. It represents the reduction in monthly violent events attributable to iTSCi, holding constant time-invariant cell characteristics and common monthly shocks. The effect is local (applies only where iTSCi operated) and conditional (depends on iTSCi's 4-pillar intervention model remaining in place). It does not measure aggregate regional violence trends, which reflect multiple simultaneous conflicts beyond DD's scope.

These case studies examine demilitarization processes at two major cassiterite mining sites in Eastern DRC, illustrating how military interventions, governance reforms, and supply chain mechanisms interact to reduce armed group presence at mine sites.

Cross-Case Insights
✓ Common Patterns
  • Military force alone insufficient—needed governance + market mechanisms
  • State forces replacing militias ≠ demilitarization (rent-extraction continues, though evidence suggests FARDC taxation is more systematic and less violent than non-state militia extortion)
  • Both sites took 4-6 years of sustained intervention (2009-2015) to reach stability
⚠ Critical Difference
Nyabibwe: iTSCi pilot program (traceability + market incentives) → "Certification brought us peace"
Bisie: Industrial mining company (MPC) → Created new artisanal vs. LSM conflicts
Ongoing challenge: FARDC presence creates governance problems even after militia expulsion
Case Study 1: Bisie Mining Site, Walikale Territory, North Kivu
Largest cassiterite deposit in DRC — Multi-phased demilitarization (2006-2015)
Gonzalez Torres et al. (2025), OECD DRC Report, Appendix D
📍 Location: Bisie, Walikale Territory, North Kivu Province
View Larger Map | Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors
Context:
• Remote, mountainous location
• Largest cassiterite deposit in DRC
• Discovered 2002
• ~100km from major population centers

Coordinates:
Approx. 1°12'S, 28°18'E
(Walikale Territory)
Key Takeaways:
1. Multi-phased military interventions were necessary but insufficient alone
  • 2006-2009: Maï-Maï militia (Colonel Sammy Matumo) control → Monthly taxes of ~$120,000
  • 2009: FARDC command restructuring created unintended consequence: Maï-Maï Sheka formation
  • August 2009: Military campaign pushed FDLR back but didn't eliminate them—they adapted tactics to attacking mines from forest bases
  • 2010-2012: Multiple waves needed as FDLR, Maï-Maï Sheka, and FARDC brigades battled for control
2. Industrial mining created new tensions alongside armed groups
  • 2013-2014: Mining and Processing Congo (MPC) vs. artisanal miners conflict
  • November 2013: Artisanal miners protested forced eviction; police violence (3 injured by gunfire, station ransacked)
  • July 2014: NDC-Sheka attack on MPC facilities; cooperatives (COMIMPA, COMINDER, COCABI) suspended
  • March 2015: Police used excessive force during eviction (26 dwellings destroyed, 100 tons cassiterite looted)
3. Successful outcome required military + non-military integration
  • July 2014: FARDC-MONUSCO joint offensive successfully displaced NDC-Sheka from multiple territories
  • August 2014: Provincial Governor suspended cooperative activities and evicted artisanal diggers
  • 2015: Series of negotiations between MPC and artisanal miners led to peaceful coexistence at mine sites
  • September 2015: iTSCi Security Report classified Bisie as LOW-RISK due to public security forces presence and absence of security/human rights incidents
4. Limitations: State rent-extraction replaced militia taxation (though less volatile)
FARDC presence at mines creates governance problem: state security forces replacing non-state militias doesn't eliminate rent-extraction, it merely shifts who collects. However, evidence suggests FARDC taxation is more systematic and less violent than non-state militia extortion—DDP areas showed "fewer instances of irregular taxation" and less use of physical force compared to militia-controlled sites (PRG et al. 2020; IPIS/ULULA 2019). Still falls outside supply-chain leverage mechanisms.
📖 Detailed Case Narrative

Background (2002-2006)

The Bisie mining site, located in North Kivu's Walikale territory, lies in a mountainous and forested landscape. This remote setting isolates the site, making it poorly connected—a geography that favors the refuge of armed groups (Franciscans International, 2017). Bisie is the largest cassiterite deposit in the DRC (Garrett, 2008). Artisanal mining began in 2002 amid relatively low levels of tension and armed conflict. Since its discovery, the region has continually faced conflict and human rights abuses.

⚔️ Takeaway Link → Multi-phased military interventions: The 2006-2009 period marked the beginning of militia control that would require repeated military interventions over nearly a decade.

First Military Phase: Maï-Maï Control (2006-2009)

In 2006, the Maï-Maï militia led by Colonel Sammy Matumo seized control of the mine and maintained it until 2009. During this period, the militia—which later integrated into the Congolese national army (FARDC, 85th brigade)—imposed monthly production taxes on the mine totaling approximately US$120,000 (Global Witness, 2009).

The Congolese government's initial demilitarization involved reassigning territory to the "integrated" 1st Brigade (ex-CNDP FARDC brigade). However, this created unintended consequences: soldiers and deserters from the 85th Brigade, along with participants in the tin trade, coalesced to form Maï-Maï Sheka. This group allied with the FDLR (Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda) to assert control over revenue from Bisie and other regional mines. Although the Congolese army oversaw the site from 2006 to 2009, it faced allegations of extorting cassiterite and taxes from miners (Geenen & Custers, 2010).

Second Military Phase: August 2009 Campaign

A major military campaign in August 2009 aimed to repel armed groups from mining sites and weaken them financially and militarily (Crisis Group, 2009). While these actions succeeded in pushing back the FDLR, they did not significantly weaken the group. Instead, the FDLR retreated deeper into the forest, relinquishing some mining sites but adapting their strategy to focus on attacking mining areas from forest bases (Wimmer & Hilgert, 2011).

⚔️ Takeaway Link → Military interventions insufficient alone: Armed groups adapted tactics rather than disbanding—demonstrating that military force alone cannot achieve lasting demilitarization.

Continued Instability (2010-2012)

Starting in 2010, Bisie became a battleground for the FDLR, Mayi-Mayi Sheka, and the ex-CNDP FARDC brigade. Their frequent raids disrupted cassiterite trade, causing traders to flee (iTSCi, 2015). In July 2010, the government attempted to replace the brigade overseeing the site, but several elements refused to leave. In September 2010, the president announced a ban on artisanal exploitation, leading to a new FARDC military operation in Walikale territory. This ban was lifted in March 2011, coinciding with a major military restructuring in the Kivu provinces, including withdrawing brigades from mine areas (UN Secretary-General, 2011; Global Witness, 2011). By February 2012, the legitimate mining police began asserting control, and the regular Congolese army ultimately regained control over the Bisie mining sites (Wimmer & Hilgert, 2011; Franciscans International, 2017).

Industrial Mining Conflicts (2013-2014)

In 2013, Bisie found itself once again under armed group control. In November 2013, artisanal miners protested their forced eviction from the site in favor of Mining and Processing Congo (MPC), an industrial mining company. The mining police response was marked by violence: three protesters sustained injuries from gunfire, and angered demonstrators retaliated by ransacking the mine police station.

On July 16, 2014, an armed group suspected to be the Nduma Defense of Congo (NDC)—led by Ntabo Ntaberi Sheka—launched an attack on MPC facilities. The attack resulted in burning and looting of MPC facilities, and in retaliation, several cases of torture, inhuman treatment, arbitrary arrests, and illegal detentions of artisanal miners occurred. Allegations emerged of links between mining cooperatives and the armed group, whose common goal was to destabilize MPC's activities (Franciscans International, 2017).

⚔️ Takeaway Link → Industrial mining created new tensions: The transition from ASM to LSM created a new axis of conflict between artisanal miners, cooperatives, industrial operators, and armed groups exploiting the chaos.

Third Military Phase: FARDC-MONUSCO Operations (July 2014)

To demilitarize the area and remove NDC armed groups, the Congolese government initiated a military offensive in collaboration with MONUSCO (United Nations) and the FARDC in July 2014. This joint military effort successfully displaced NDC-Sheka forces from several groupements in Walikale, including Luberiki, Wassa, and Ihana (iTSCi, 2015). The coordinated FARDC-MONUSCO operations played a crucial role in stabilizing the Walikale region.

Given cooperatives' alleged involvement in the MPC attack, the Governor of North Kivu Province suspended activities by three cooperatives (COMIMPA, COMINDER, and COCABI) on MPC concessions in August 2014 and ordered eviction of artisanal diggers from the site. Courts in Walikale issued arrest warrants against artisanal miners and cooperative members accused of looting and damaging MPC (IPIS, 2016).

Negotiations and Peaceful Coexistence (March 2015)

In March 2015, a dispute with MPC concerning drill installation prompted cooperative members to stage protests and mobilize to the mining company's camp. In response, the administrator of Walikale territory ordered eviction of all artisanal miners from the 45-minute site. During this eviction attempt, police faced accusations of using excessive force against unarmed individuals, resulting in injuries to a dozen people, destruction of 26 temporary dwellings, and looting of 100 tons of cassiterite (IPIS, 2016).

Subsequent to these events, a series of negotiations took place, leading to the peaceful coexistence of both MPC and artisanal miners at Bisie mining sites. Observations from the iTSCi Bisie Security Report indicated that rebel involvement in Bisie mining was limited in 2015 and 2016, supported by IPIS studies (iTSCi, 2015; IPIS, 2016).

✓ Takeaway Link → Successful outcome required military + non-military integration: The combination of FARDC-MONUSCO operations, cooperative suspensions, and crucially, negotiations between MPC and artisanal miners, created the conditions for stability.

Outcome: Low-Risk Classification (September 2015)

By September 2015, Bisie was classified as a low-risk mining site due to the presence of public security forces and the absence of security and human rights-related incidents (iTSCi, 2015). This outcome was achieved through both military and non-military strategies: restructuring FARDC command, conducting interventions to combat armed groups (at times with MONUSCO collaboration), and implementing non-military measures to restructure and secure the mining site while excluding private actors who had been colluding with rebels.

⚠ Takeaway Link → State rent-extraction replaced militia taxation: While Bisie achieved low-risk status, FARDC presence at mines creates ongoing governance problems. State security forces replacing non-state militias doesn't eliminate rent-extraction—it merely shifts who collects, falling outside supply-chain leverage. However, evidence suggests FARDC taxation is more systematic and predictable, with DDP areas showing "fewer instances of irregular taxation" and less use of physical violence compared to non-state militia extortion (PRG et al. 2020; IPIS/ULULA 2019).
Case Study 2: Nyabibwe (Kalimbi Mine), Kalehe Territory, South Kivu
iTSCi pilot site — Ethnic conflict + traceability (2003-2013)
Gonzalez Torres et al. (2025), OECD DRC Report, Appendix D
📍 Location: Nyabibwe, Kalehe Territory, South Kivu Province
View Larger Map | Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors
Context:
• Main Goma-Bukavu road (Lake Kivu shore)
• Kalimbi mine: primary cassiterite site
• High ethnic diversity
• Strategic transport corridor

Coordinates:
Approx. 2°03'S, 28°51'E
(Kalehe Territory, along Lake Kivu)
Key Takeaways:
1. Ethnic conflict + mining cooperatives = complex violence
  • Indigenous (Tembo, Havu) vs. Banyarwanda (Hutu, Tutsi) tensions since 1950s settlement
  • Land competition over abundant cassiterite deposits drove ethnic confrontations
  • 2009-2010: Cooperative rivalries (COMBECKA vs. COMIKA) turned violent with armed factions
  • Third cooperative (COMILAK) formed during chaos, creating 3-way conflict over mine control
2. Military operations controlled territory but created new problems
  • 2003: Global and Inclusive Peace Agreement → partial integration of Mai-Mai and RCD into FARDC
  • 2007: Dissatisfied soldiers rejected integration → formed Kirikicho Mai-Mai, Mai-Mai Kifuafua, PARECO
  • 2009: Operations "Umoja Wetu," "Kimya 2," "Amani Leo" targeted FDLR (2,000+ members in Kalehe)
  • By 2009: FARDC controlled Kalimbi mine but imposed weekly $100 fees on diggers—state rent-extraction replaced militia taxation
3. iTSCi traceability pilot site brought peace (June 2010)
  • June 2010: Nyabibwe selected as ITRI Tin Supply Chain Initiative (iTSCi) pilot site
  • Collaboration with SAESSCAM and Mining Division to implement bagging/tagging system
  • Each mineral shipment required comprehensive documentation at every trading step
  • Strong support from Minerals Supply Africa (MSA), the largest mineral buyer in eastern DRC
  • Local priest testimony: "Mayi-Mayi village militias have long been a presence. Certification has finally brought us peace and security."
  • By February 2013: ITRI reported great success with over 200 tons of tin ore exported
4. Success factors: Traceability + stakeholder buy-in + market access
iTSCi worked because: (1) Major buyer (MSA) supported it, creating market incentives; (2) Multi-stakeholder engagement (cooperatives, government, civil society); (3) Excluded illegal supply chains while providing legitimate market access. This demonstrates supply chain mechanisms can contribute to demilitarization when combined with market pressure and local governance.
📖 Detailed Case Narrative

Background: Geography and Ethnic Diversity

Nyabibwe, a village in Kalehe territory within South Kivu province, stands along the main road tracing the shores of Lake Kivu—a pivotal route connecting Goma (North Kivu's primary town) and Bukavu (South Kivu's main town) (Ansoms, Claessens, & Mudinga, 2011). This strategic location makes Nyabibwe important for regional commerce and communication.

Characterized by substantial cultural diversity, Nyabibwe hosts multiple ethnic groups: Bahavu, Batembo, Barongeronge, Hutu, Tutsi, Bahunde, and others. While the Hutus form the largest demographic, the Havu, Tembo, Bashi, and Tutsi communities also contribute to Nyabibwe's population (APC/Life & Peace Institute, 2008). The village, nestled in the Buhavu Chiefdom of Kalehe Territory, bears historical tensions between the Hutus on one side and the Tembo and Havu on the other—a conflict rekindled by prevailing dynamics of strife and militarization.

Positioned in an area abundant with significant cassiterite deposits, Nyabibwe's prominence is accentuated by the Kalimbi mine, the primary cassiterite mining site in the region. This mining potential places the village and entire territory in land competition and confrontations among different ethnic communities (Cuvelier, 2010).

⚔️ Takeaway Link → Ethnic conflict + mining cooperatives: The indigenous-allochthonous divide, centered on Banyarwanda (Hutu/Tutsi) settlement since the 1950s, became intertwined with competition over cassiterite resources.

Conflict Dynamics: Ethnic Communities, Armed Groups, and Cooperatives

The diversity of ethnic communities in Kalehe gives rise to distinctive attitudes that perpetuate the indigenous-allochthonous divide. Frustrations within the population often center on the influx of Banyarwanda (Hutus and Tutsis) who have settled in the region since the 1950s. This demographic tension intersects with armed group dynamics and cooperative rivalries to create complex conflict patterns.

In 2007, of the 6,000 to 7,000 FDLR members in the two Kivu provinces, no less than 2,000 were operating in Kalehe. The FDLR comprises former Rwandan army (ex-FAR) members, extremist Hutu militias (Interahamwe), and Congolese and Rwandan civilians and refugees (Cuvelier, 2010).

In July 2009, intense tensions in mine management arose between the COMBECKA and COMIKA cooperatives, culminating in a fatal confrontation in July 2010. SAESSCAM convened a meeting to reconcile the two cooperatives, asserting that neither fully met necessary conditions to manage the mine sites. Following the meeting, some COMBECKA diggers—armed and seeking to occupy the wells—encountered resistance from armed members of COMIKA, who controlled the mine during this period (Cuvelier, 2010).

Seizing the opportunity, a faction of diggers organized and established a cooperative named COMILAK, holding all pertinent official documents permitting mineral exploitation at the same site. Throughout these conflicts, the mine sites became heavily militarized, and public services (SAESSCAM, police, army) struggled to maintain control. The amalgamation of cooperative conflicts and armed group presence escalated Kalimbi's security situation to a critical level (Ansoms et al., 2011).

⚔️ Takeaway Link → Complex violence: Three-way cooperative conflicts (COMBECKA vs. COMIKA vs. COMILAK), each with armed factions, combined with FDLR presence and ethnic tensions to create interlocking security crises.

Military Approach: Peace Agreements and Operations (2003-2009)

Considering the complexities of armed groups and ethnic conflicts, negotiations unfolded following the signing of the Global and Inclusive Peace Agreement in 2003. This agreement facilitated integration of certain armed groups into the newly established FARDC. General Padiri's Mai-Mai and RCD soldiers were among those successfully integrated (Ansoms et al., 2011).

However, the post-agreement period witnessed a reconfiguration of the military landscape. As most former belligerent forces withdrew, creating a military vacuum, the FDLR capitalized on the opportunity to extend control over vast areas in northwest Kalehe territory. Simultaneously, some Mai-Mai and RCD soldiers—dissatisfied with peace agreement outcomes (insufficient rank recognition)—rejected integration. Retreating into the forest, they formed new armed groups over time: Kirikicho Mai-Mai, Mai-Mai Kifuafua, and PARECO (Patriotes Résistants Congolais) in 2007 (APC, 2008).

In response to negotiation failures and persistent armed group presence at Kalimbi mining site, the Congolese government initiated successive military operations starting January 2009: "Umoja Wetu" (Our unity), "Kimya 2" (Peace), and "Amani Leo" (Peace today). These operations aimed to root out armed groups, particularly the FDLR, in Kalehe and other territories (Cuvelier, 2010).

Although these military endeavors did not completely eliminate armed groups, by 2009, the Kalimbi mining sites had come under FARDC control. However, FARDC presence brought its own challenges: A 2009 IPIS study revealed that diggers at Kalimbi mine were compelled to pay a weekly fee of US$100 to the FARDC commander stationed there as part of "Kimya 2" operation (IPIS, 2009).

⚠ Takeaway Link → Military operations created new problems: FARDC controlled territory but imposed $100 weekly fees—state rent-extraction replaced militia taxation. However, systematic state taxation (even if extractive) is less volatile than non-state militia extortion involving "physical force" and arbitrary violence (Nyatura militias demanded $2,000/week plus entire day's production—UN 2020). Demonstrates limits of military-only approaches.

Non-Military Approach: iTSCi Pilot Site (June 2010)

Another crucial factor contributing to Kalimbi mine demilitarization was the selection of Nyabibwe by ITRI as the pilot site for its traceability project: the ITRI Tin Supply Chain Initiative (iTSCi). Starting from the end of June 2010, iTSCi personnel collaborated with SAESSCAM and the Congolese Mining Division (Division des Mines) to implement a bagging and tagging system for mineral bags originating from Kalimbi mine.

Each shipment of minerals was required to be accompanied by comprehensive documentation, outlining every step in the trading process. During implementation, the traceability initiative received substantial support from Minerals Supply Africa (MSA), the foremost mineral buyer in eastern DRC. MSA had initially been registered in Rwanda and operated through Kigali-based company Eurotrade International SARL until early 2007, when the business relationship ended and Eurotrade ceased trading minerals from eastern DRC.

The certification process yielded positive outcomes, as emphasized by a Nyabibwe priest:

" Mayi-Mayi village militias have long been a presence in the region. Certification has finally brought us peace and security, despite our distance from Bukavu, located 100 kilometers away, or three long hours by road, given their current condition.

Furthermore, ITRI hailed the project as a great success: by February 2013, over 200 tons of tin ore had been exported from Nyabibwe through the iTSCi system.

✓ Takeaway Link → iTSCi traceability brought peace: The combination of tagging/documentation, SAESSCAM/Mining Division collaboration, and crucially, MSA buyer support created market incentives that aligned stakeholder interests toward legitimate trade.

Conclusion: Traceability as Demilitarization Mechanism

The Nyabibwe mining site has been marked by armed conflicts involving ethnic tensions, cooperative rivalries, and foreign armed groups. Military interventions were the primary demilitarization measures initially implemented. While military dynamics concluded in 2009 with FARDC assuming control of Nyabibwe, the ongoing presence of soldiers—even if affiliated with the national army—on mining sites demands specific monitoring, as these soldiers may be susceptible to exploiting mines for personal gain.

As another measure of demilitarization, Nyabibwe was chosen by ITRI as a pilot site for its traceability project. This initiative demonstrates that traceability mechanisms can indeed contribute to the demilitarization process, especially with support from various stakeholders: government services (SAESSCAM, Mining Division), major buyers (MSA), and local cooperatives that gained legitimate market access.

✓ Takeaway Link → Success factors: iTSCi worked because (1) Major buyer supported it, creating market incentives; (2) Multi-stakeholder engagement; (3) Excluded illegal supply chains while providing legitimate access. This demonstrates supply chain mechanisms can contribute to demilitarization when combined with market pressure and local governance—but only when major buyers commit to purchasing compliant minerals.
Methodology & Sources: These case studies synthesize evidence from multiple sources: IPIS mine visit databases, iTSCi security reports and incident tracking data, UN Group of Experts reports on the DRC, ACLED conflict event data, and secondary literature on Eastern DRC mining conflicts. The Bisie narrative draws primarily on iTSCi Bisie Security Reports (2015), IPIS Third Party Reviews (2016), Wimmer & Hilgert (2011), and Franciscans International (2017). The Nyabibwe narrative draws on Cuvelier (2010), Ansoms et al. (2011), APC/Life & Peace Institute reports, and IPIS mine mapping data. Comparative analysis of state vs. non-state taxation draws on PRG, IPIS, SFR, and Ulula (2020) and IPIS/Ulula (2019). Full case study details and additional references available in Gonzalez Torres, E., Christensen, D., Park, D., Geuna, T., Cubaka, P.M., & Bayer, C. (2025). Evaluation of the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas: Democratic Republic of the Congo. OECD Report, Appendix Section D.

iTSCi (ITRI Tin Supply Chain Initiative)
Mine traceability coverage data by province, 2014–2022. iTSCi operates a 4-pillar intervention programme at enrolled mines: (1) continuous monitoring & traceability (bagging/tagging), (2) incident reporting mechanism, (3) multi-stakeholder committees (local/provincial risk mitigation forums), (4) joint risk mitigation measures (sanctions, deterrence, community policing).
→ itsci.org
BGR (Bundesanstalt für Geowissenschaften und Rohstoffe)
DRC Mine Certification Programme. Qualification status (Green/Yellow/Red) for artisanal mining sites.
→ bgr.bund.de

Frameworks & Methodologies

OECD (2016)
OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas, 3rd Edition. OECD Publishing, Paris.
→ View PDF
The foundational guidance establishing the 5-step due diligence framework and Annex II risk categories (serious human rights abuses, conflict finance, financial crimes). Defines company responsibilities for identifying and mitigating risks in mineral supply chains from conflict-affected and high-risk areas. Global in scope, applicable to all minerals.
OECD (2022)
Monitoring and Evaluation Framework for the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas. OECD Publishing, Paris.
→ View PDF
Official theory of change and evaluation framework for the OECD DDG, used as the foundation for this analysis.
Parker, D. P., & Vadheim, B. (2017)
"Resource Cursed or Policy Cursed? US Regulation of Conflict Minerals and Violence in the Congo." Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists, 4(1), 1-49.
Critiques the "balloon effect" — displacement of violence when armed groups lose mineral revenue.
Stoop, N., Verpoorten, M., & van der Windt, P. (2018)
"More Legislation, More Violence? The Impact of Dodd-Frank in the DRC." PLOS ONE, 13(8), e0201783.
Documents displacement effects and unintended consequences of conflict mineral regulations.
Mizuno, T., Ohnishi, T., & Watanabe, T. (2016)
"Structure of Global Buyer-Supplier Networks and its Implications for Conflict Minerals Regulations." EPJ Data Science, 5(1), 2.
→ View article
Network analysis of 400,000 global firms showing how conflict minerals flow through multi-hop supply chains from DRC to end markets. Demonstrates "six degrees of separation" between mines and consumers, with minerals flowing through smelter hubs (notably Malaysia, Thailand) before reaching China and G8 countries. Simulates regulatory interventions targeting strategic network nodes. Foundational work on supply chain complexity and mineral flow modeling.
Geenen, S., & Claessens, K. (2016)
"Disputed Access to the Gold Sites in Luhwindja, Eastern DRC." Journal of Modern African Studies, 54(1), 85-108.
Case study on local resistance to formalization and the limits of supply-chain interventions.
IPIS/Ulula (2019)
Assessing the Impact of Due Diligence Programmes in Eastern DRC: A Baseline Study. IPIS Report, April 2019.
→ IPIS Research
Baseline study comparing DDP vs. non-DDP mining sites. Found fewer instances of irregular taxation and illegal taxation by FARDC/armed groups in DDP areas. Documents systematic differences in state vs. non-state taxation patterns at mine sites.
PRG, IPIS, SFR, and Ulula (2020)
Evaluating Due Diligence Programs for Conflict Minerals: A Matched Analysis of 3T Mines in Eastern DRC. Los Angeles and Antwerp.
Comprehensive matched-pair analysis of DDP effectiveness. Found improved legal taxation and state service presence in DDP areas, with households reporting "less FARDC presence and related taxation" compared to non-DDP areas. Documents shift from violent militia extortion to more systematic (though still extractive) state taxation.
Stoop, N., Verpoorten, M., & van der Windt, P. (2018)
"More Legislation, More Violence? The Impact of Dodd-Frank in the DRC." PLoS ONE, 13(8).
Documents displacement effects from 3T to gold mining sectors following Dodd-Frank implementation.
Parker, D. P., & Vadheim, B. (2017)
"Resource Cursed or Policy Cursed? US Regulation of Conflict Minerals and Violence in the Congo." Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists, 4(1), 1-49.
Examines unintended consequences of conflict minerals regulation and armed group displacement to unregulated sectors.

Primary Research Report

Gonzalez Torres, E., Christensen, D., Park, D., Geuna, T., Cubaka, P.M., & Bayer, C. (2025)
Evaluation of the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas: Democratic Republic of the Congo. OECD Publication.
Comprehensive evaluation of due diligence mechanisms in the DRC's 3T sector (2010-2022). Features econometric analysis using difference-in-differences methodology showing 61% reduction in violent incidents at iTSCi-enrolled mines, case studies of Bisie and Nyabibwe demilitarization processes, actor taxonomy of armed groups, analysis of smelter compliance, and assessment of socio-economic impacts on mining communities. This dashboard synthesizes key findings from the report with interactive data visualizations.

Dashboard & Analysis

This interactive dashboard and the accompanying empirical analysis were developed as part of ongoing research into the effectiveness of supply-chain due diligence interventions in conflict-affected regions.

Data integration, actor taxonomy, conflict typology classification, and econometric modeling. The 61% treatment-effect estimate referenced in the Overview tab is derived from proprietary IPIS mine-level panel data using difference-in-differences specifications. Full methodology and results are published in: Gonzalez Torres, E., Christensen, D., Park, D., Geuna, T., Cubaka, P.M., & Bayer, C. (2025). Evaluation of the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas: Democratic Republic of the Congo. OECD Report, Section C.
